questions.q: What does the lesson mean by 'a diagram is a claim, not a guarantee'?
options: Diagrams are legally binding documents once approved in a design review
A diagram shows intended behavior, not verified behavior — every arrow and box should be read skeptically, not taken as proof
Diagrams should never be used in a design review at all
Only Terraform-generated diagrams can be trusted; hand-drawn ones cannot
questions.explain: A box or arrow describes how the system is supposed to behave, not confirmation that it behaves that way — a reader has to question what the picture isn't showing.

questions.q: While tracing one request through a diagram, which pattern does the lesson call out as a reliability concern worth flagging on sight?
options: A single inbound arrow that fans out to five internal services, each able to independently fail the whole request
A diagram that uses dashed lines for trust boundaries
An arrow labeled with the name of the cloud provider
A box drawn in a different color than the others
questions.explain: An inbound request fanning out to multiple services, any of which can fail the whole request, is exactly the kind of reliability risk the first trace pass is designed to surface.

questions.q: At every trust boundary crossing on a diagram, what two questions does the lesson say to ask every time?
options: What color is the arrow, and does it match the vendor's branding guide
How many boxes are inside the boundary, and who drew the diagram
Which cloud region is shown, and what time zone it operates in
What enforces this boundary, and is that enforcement visible on the diagram or just assumed
questions.explain: The lesson's repeatable check at every boundary crossing is identifying the enforcement mechanism (NSG, private endpoint, identity check, firewall) and whether it's actually shown or only assumed.

questions.q: Why might two components drawn as separate boxes on a diagram still share the same failure domain in practice?
options: Because diagrams are always drawn to scale
Because separate boxes are never actually allowed in a Well-Architected design
Because they both depend on the same underlying infrastructure — such as a single-region database or shared availability zone — regardless of how far apart the diagram draws them
Because the diagram's line thickness determines failure domain boundaries
questions.explain: A failure domain is determined by shared underlying infrastructure, not by visual separation — components drawn apart can still fail together if they depend on the same database, queue, or zone.

questions.q: What is the overall skill this lesson builds toward, once data flow, trust boundaries, and failure domains have all been traced on a diagram?
options: Memorizing every label on the diagram word for word
Translating what's visible on the diagram directly into the same specific, pillar-anchored review language practiced in Lessons 2 and 3, without needing config files first
Redrawing the diagram using only Azure-native icon sets
Rejecting any diagram that doesn't show every trust boundary explicitly
questions.explain: The chapter's throughline is turning a picture into concrete pillar findings — fan-out, unguarded boundary crossings, shared failure domains — in the same specific language used throughout the design review in Lessons 2 and 3.
